title: The Counter on Bolivar: an Importer of Machines and the First Argentine Century of Film and Shellac
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Czernowitz, the birth on the edge of the empire
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: In Czernowitz, capital of Austrian Bukovina, Mordechai David Glücksmann is born into a city where German, Yiddish, Romanian and Ruthenian are spoken in the same street and nearly a third of the inhabitants are Jews. Vienna governs the province from a thousand miles off; the Prut marks the edge of the empire. Nothing in the town points toward a machine that makes pictures move, or toward a river a hemisphere south. At fifteen he leaves for a port he has never seen, in a country whose language he cannot speak, and he does not come back.
suggested_refs: Habsburg Czernowitz before 1890, the Jewish quarter and the German-language schools

stops.name: Port of Buenos Aires, the landing
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unrecorded, and no source consulted names the ship or the berth
stops.campa: The ship docks at Buenos Aires and a fifteen-year-old from Bukovina walks down onto a wharf built for a decade of mass arrivals: Italians, Spaniards, Poles, Syrians, all funnelled through the same customs sheds and the same questions. No manifest naming his vessel survives in the sources consulted, and the exact berth is a reconstruction. Within months he is behind a counter on Avenida Bolivar handling glass plates and chemicals. This city will be his only address for the next fifty-six years.
suggested_refs: Argentine immigration registers of 1890, Puerto Madero and the old Dársena Sur

stops.name: Casa Lepage, the photography assistant
stops.date_confidence: c. 1891; ES Wikipedia dates the job to 1890 in the same sentence in which it dates Lepage's own arrival to 1891, a contradiction left standing in the source; EN says only shortly after his arrival
stops.campa: At Casa Lepage, Bolivar 375, the boy is taken on as a photographic assistant to Enrique Lepage, who runs the first shop in Argentina importing apparatus for filming and projection. A Frenchman works the same rooms, Eugenio Py, who will shoot the country's earliest surviving footage; the two keep the same counter for eighteen years. Glücksmann learns the trade upward from the plate: lenses, emulsions, the shipping of fragile things across an ocean, the names of the houses in Paris and Lyon that make them. The building still stands.
suggested_refs: The Casa Lepage premises at Bolivar 375, Monserrat, with its commemorative plaque

stops.name: Teatro Odeon, the first cinematograph in Argentina
stops.date_confidence: day disputed: ES Wikipedia 'Max Glucksmann' gives 18 July 1896, EN 'Cinema of Argentina' and eugene_py.journey.json give 28 July 1896; not resolved
stops.campa: On Esmeralda near Corrientes, in a house built five years earlier for the brewer Emilio Bieckert, Lumiere footage is thrown on a screen before an audience that has never seen a photograph move. Glücksmann is there with Lepage and Py. Afterward the three approach the Lumiere company to buy the apparatus and the conversations fail; they turn instead to Gaumont-Demeny and to Pathe. The Odeon is pulled down in 1991, and a tower of thirty-seven storeys now stands on the ground where that audience sat.
suggested_refs: The Teatro Odeon (1891-1991), Ferdinand Moog architect, demolished; Torre Odeon on the site since 2019

stops.name: Casa Lepage, the order that goes to Paris instead
stops.date_confidence: year attested for the Cronofotografo Elge import; month and day unrecorded
stops.campa: Refused at Lyon, the shop on Bolivar orders from Paris: a Cronofotografo Elge, the Gaumont-Demeny machine, which crosses the Atlantic in 1897 while Glücksmann stays behind his counter. He handles the crates, the spare parts, the stock, the correspondence in three languages. A national cinema is assembled in its first decade out of a catalogue, a bank draft, a ship, and four or five men in one room deciding what a country of four million people will be shown.
suggested_refs: Gaumont-Demeny Chronophotographe sales records for the River Plate, 1896-1898

stops.name: Plaza de Mayo, the flag over the square
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unrecorded
stops.campa: With the Gaumont camera out of its crate, Py turns it on the Argentine flag flying over the Plaza de Mayo and exposes some seventeen metres of film. It is counted as the first film made in Argentina, and it is made with equipment Glücksmann ordered, received and mounted. He is twenty-two, on wages, and the square is four blocks from the shop where he works. The halls, the labels, the newsreels and the plant in Belgrano are all thirty years off, and the trade that pays for them starts with this length of exposed film.
suggested_refs: Eugenio Py, 'La bandera argentina' (1897), roughly 17 metres, Gaumont camera

stops.name: Casa Lepage, the rooster of Pathe
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the Pathe import is undated in the sources and is placed here only as following the 1897 Gaumont order
stops.campa: Alongside the Gaumont line the shop adds machines from Pathe Freres, in a year the sources do not record. Glücksmann distributes both from Bolivar, the rooster and the tulip, and the reels that come with them: Paris streets, a train, a coronation, a boxing match. Buenos Aires sees the world outside Argentina flicker on a wall because a clerk from Czernowitz knows which house in France sells which part. He owns none of it. The stock and the halls belong to other men, and every one of them has to ask him where the reels and the spare lamps come from.
suggested_refs: Compania General de Fonografos, Cinematografos y Aparatos de Precision, Pathe's River Plate distributor

stops.name: Salon Nacional, Maipu 471
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unrecorded
stops.campa: At Maipu 471 the Salon Nacional opens, the first hall in the country built to show films and nothing else. Glücksmann supplies the trade it belongs to without owning any of it yet: the machines, the spare parts, the imported reels. Nineteen years on he will raise a far grander house on Avenida Santa Fe and it will be called the first cinema in Argentina by people who have forgotten this address. The exhibition business he comes to dominate across four countries opens its first door here, without him.
suggested_refs: The Salon Nacional at Maipu 471, Argentina's first dedicated film hall

stops.name: Santiago de Chile, the arbitration filmed for him
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unrecorded
stops.campa: Glücksmann decides that Eugenio Py and the journalist Enrique Casellas shall cross the Andes to film the boundary arbitration between Argentina and Chile, judged by Sir Thomas Holdich under a commission from Edward VII. The camera goes over the Uspallata pass by mule and rail. Glücksmann stays in Buenos Aires and pays for it. He is still nominally an employee of another man's shop, and he is already choosing the subject, dispatching the operator and keeping the negative. The habit does not change in forty years.
stops.quote: En 1902 Max Glucksmann decidio que Eugenio Py y un periodista espanol, Enrique Casellas, viajaran al pais trasandino
stops.quote_source: Quoted in eugene_py.journey.json, stop on the Andes filming trip (Spanish source relayed through that file, accents as transcribed there)
suggested_refs: The 1902 Argentina-Chile boundary arbitration before Sir Thomas Holdich

segments.name: Shellac, and the Purchase of the Firm

stops.name: Berlin, the label he never visits
stops.date_confidence: EN 'Odeon Records' dates the label's founding to 1903; the Glücksmann articles date it to 1904, which is the year of his agency; the discrepancy is left standing
stops.campa: In Berlin, Max Straus and Heinrich Zuntz of the International Talking Machine Company put out a label they name Odeon, after a theatre in Paris. Neither man ever meets Glücksmann, as far as the record shows; the tie between the Prussian pressing plant and the shop in Buenos Aires is a contract and a shipping manifest. From Buenos Aires an immigrant from Bukovina will decide what the Berlin presses stamp into shellac for the River Plate and the countries above it, and he will never see the presses.
suggested_refs: International Talking Machine Company, Berlin-Weissensee, and the Odeon trademark

stops.name: Buenos Aires, agent for Odeon
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unrecorded
stops.campa: Glücksmann takes the Argentine agency for Odeon: the machines and the discs, imported by the crate, sold from his own counters. Sound is a second trade laid over the first, and it turns out to be the more durable one. A film is rented, shown and sent back scratched; a record is bought and kept in a house. Within ten years the second trade is worth more to him than every hall he owns, and it is still his on the day he dies, seventeen years after the halls have gone.
suggested_refs: Odeon Records agency contracts for the River Plate, from 1904

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the royalty nobody else pays
stops.date_confidence: the sources date the founding of Discos Glücksmann only to the 1900s; the year here is a placement within that decade
stops.campa: He founds his own label, Discos Glücksmann, and Odeon builds him a pressing and processing plant in Buenos Aires. Then he does the thing nobody in the country does: he pays composers and performers a royalty on every copy sold instead of a flat fee for the session. It makes him very rich, and it makes him liked by the musicians, which is not the usual outcome for a man who ends up owning the industry that sells their voices. Tango is not yet the music of the city. He signs it anyway, and early.
suggested_refs: Discos Glucksmann label catalogues and the Odeon-built pressing plant in Buenos Aires

stops.name: Casa Lepage, the firm bought outright
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unrecorded
stops.campa: Enrique Lepage steps back and Glücksmann buys the business entire. The shop where he was taken on at fifteen carries his own name over the door at thirty-three, and Py, who has worked beside him for eighteen years, now works for him. From this address the expansion runs outward fast: halls in the capital, halls in the interior, halls over two borders and then a third. He owns the counter he was hired to stand behind at fifteen, and within a few years the screens its stock is projected on.
suggested_refs: The 1908 transfer of Casa Lepage to Max Glucksmann

stops.name: The Argentine interior, halls without names
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the sources attest expansion into the interior from 1908 onward but name no town and no year, and the position is the country's geographic centre standing for all of them
stops.campa: Beyond Buenos Aires the circuit reaches into the provincial towns, and the sources name not one of them. The pattern repeats for two decades: a hall opens, his newsreels and his imported features fill the programme, and a place that had no moving pictures has them because a single importer in the capital decided it should. How many halls is itself contested. One account says more than sixty across four countries; another says a hundred; the English record gives no figure at all.
suggested_refs: Provincial exhibition circuits of the Casa Glucksmann, 1908-1929

stops.name: Montevideo, the other bank
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: Uruguay is attested as a country of operation from 1908 onward, but no source names the first hall or the year it opened
stops.campa: Across the rio the circuit takes root in Montevideo, one of the four countries his halls eventually cover with Argentina, Paraguay and Chile. No source names the first Uruguayan hall or the year of its opening. Everything moves in one direction. Films, discs, machines and later a competition for singers travel outward from a single shop in Buenos Aires, and the two banks of the Plata are worked from the start as one market. Nobody in Montevideo is asked whether they agree.
suggested_refs: Montevideo exhibition halls under the Glucksmann circuit
sources: Wikipedia (EN/ES), 'Max Glücksmann' (country attested, venue not named)

stops.name: Asuncion, upriver
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: Paraguay is attested as a country of operation, but city, venue and year are unrecorded
stops.campa: In Asuncion, as in Montevideo and in Santiago over the mountains, the network extends without the sources naming a hall, a street or a date. The details are missing; the shape is not. Out of one shop in Buenos Aires go the reels, the projectors, the spare lamps and the men who know how to thread them, by rail and by river steamer, until audiences in Paraguay are watching newsreels stamped with the name of a man from Czernowitz who has never been in a room with any of them.
suggested_refs: River-steamer distribution of film prints up the Parana and Paraguay rivers
sources: Wikipedia (EN/ES), 'Max Glücksmann' (country attested, venue a reconstruction)

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the only competitor marginalised
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unrecorded
stops.campa: By 1914 he has the Argentine recording industry to himself. The method is not price but paper: exclusive long-term contracts with musicians and songwriters, signed early and renewed, which leave his one competitor, Victor, holding a catalogue with nobody left to fill it. A claim circulates that Fortune magazine listed his fortune that year. It cannot be true, since that magazine is not founded for another fifteen years. The record needs no embellishment anyway. He owns the voices, and he owns the machines that reproduce them.
suggested_refs: Exclusive artist contracts of the Casa Glucksmann, 1910-1920

stops.name: Teatro Colon, Amalia before the President
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Amalia, produced by Glücksmann, has its premiere at the Teatro Colon with the President of Argentina in the audience. A trade that began nineteen years earlier in a shop selling lenses and plates is received in the opera house of the republic. Fourteen years after the Salon Nacional opened on Maipu, the moving picture has stopped being a fairground novelty in Buenos Aires; it is a thing a head of state attends in evening dress, in the building where the city keeps its idea of itself.
suggested_refs: 'Amalia' (1914), premiere at the Teatro Colon, 12 December 1914

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the Chilean reel
stops.date_confidence: the trade notice is dated July 1915; the shooting and processing are undated within that year
stops.campa: The government of Chile wants a film for the exposition at San Francisco and cannot pay to have one made at home. The house of Max Glücksmann shoots it and develops it in Buenos Aires, and a Santiago trade paper records the fact in a paragraph, as a matter of course. Eighteen years after he was a clerk taking delivery of French crates, a foreign state comes to his laboratory because there is nowhere nearer to go. The propaganda of one country is manufactured in the capital of another.
stops.quote: ...fue mandada a imprimir por el Gobierno chileno para ser enviada a Estados Unidos, ya que la situación del erario nacional no podía hacerse representar como hubiera sido de desear. Este film fue tomado por la Casa Max Glucksmann y desarrollado en Buenos Aires.
stops.quote_source: Cine Gaceta, Prospecto Gratuito (July 1915), article 'Peliculas Nacionales', item 1, quoted in Eduardo Santa Cruz A., 'Cultura de Masas y Espacio Publico en Chile. Las Revistas de Cine (1910-1920)', Comunicacion y Medios 15 (2004), p. 145, footnote 18
suggested_refs: Chilean government film for the 1915 Panama-Pacific International Exposition, San Francisco
sources: Eduardo Santa Cruz A., Comunicacion y Medios 15 (2004), p. 145 (DOI 10.5354/rcm.v0i15.12089)

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Gardel and Razzano under contract
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unrecorded
stops.campa: He signs the duo of Carlos Gardel and Jose Razzano to an exclusive contract, and across these same years Ignacio Corsini, Roberto Firpo and Francisco Canaro. It is a transaction and not a performance: terms, a term of years, signatures in an office. The consequence is that the voice which will carry the tango to Paris and New York belongs, on paper, to a catalogue assembled by a man who came off a ship at fifteen unable to ask directions in Spanish.
suggested_refs: Glucksmann's exclusive recording contracts with Gardel-Razzano, Corsini, Firpo and Canaro

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Mi noche triste
stops.date_confidence: year attested for the recording; the label is not named in the source, and the tie to Glucksmann's operation is a reconstruction from the exclusive contracts of the same year
stops.campa: Gardel records Mi noche triste, a lyric laid over a tango that had been an instrumental, and it sells on the order of ten thousand copies. The sources consulted do not name the label on this release, and the link to Glücksmann's operation is inference from the contracts signed the same year. The market the record makes is not in dispute. From here the tango is a thing sung, and the singing is sold on discs pressed in Buenos Aires by a house that has already bought the singer.
suggested_refs: Carlos Gardel, 'Mi noche triste' (1917), roughly 10,000 copies sold

stops.name: Avenida Santa Fe 1860, the ground broken
stops.date_confidence: construction initiated 1917 per EN and ES 'El Ateneo Grand Splendid'; the research chronology dated the commission to 1919, which is the year of the dome and the opening, and the discrepancy is left standing
stops.campa: On a site that had held the Teatro Nacional Norte and a carriage works, Glücksmann commissions a house for pictures and stage at once. Pero and Torres Armengol draw it; the firm of Pizoney and Falcope builds it. The neighbourhood is called, with some irony, the Saint Germain of Buenos Aires. Twenty-seven years after the wharf, the immigrant who could not order a meal in Spanish is deciding what the grandest theatre in the capital will look like, and paying for it out of rented film and pressed shellac.
suggested_refs: Building permits and plans for the Cine Teatro Grand Splendid, Av. Santa Fe 1860

stops.name: Grand Splendid, the dome
stops.date_confidence: year attested for the completion of the dome; month and day unrecorded
stops.campa: Under the roof the Italian decorator Nazareno Orlandi paints the cupola: allegorical figures spread over the ceiling of a room built to be dark. It is the most expensive gesture in the building and the least necessary, and it is the one that survives everything else. Glücksmann is buying permanence with money made from a medium rented by the week and returned scratched. Eight decades on, that ceiling is what strangers photograph in a room where nothing is projected any more.
suggested_refs: Nazareno Orlandi's painted cupola, Grand Splendid, 1919

stops.name: Grand Splendid, the figures under the dome
stops.date_confidence: year attested for the sculptural work; month and day unrecorded
stops.campa: Troiano Troiani supplies the sculpture for the same house: caryatids, the cornice work, figures carried up the walls to meet Orlandi's ceiling. Glücksmann has hired a painter and a sculptor for a cinema, which in 1919 is not what cinemas are anywhere in the world; they are converted shops, tents, halls with a sheet at one end. On Avenida Santa Fe he is building the opposite argument in plaster and paint, that the machine he imports deserves a room made like an opera house.
suggested_refs: Troiano Troiani's caryatids and cornice ensemble, Grand Splendid

stops.name: Grand Splendid, the opening
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The doors open on the fourteenth of May: tiers of boxes, orchestra seating counted at five hundred, a house of one thousand and fifty in all, stage and screen in the same room. Gardel sings in it; Canaro plays in it; films run in it. It is called the first purpose-built cinema in Argentina, which the Salon Nacional of 1900 quietly contradicts. Twenty-nine years after the wharf, an Austro-Hungarian name is attached to the grandest theatre in the city, in a district that fancies itself Parisian.
suggested_refs: Inauguration of the Cine Teatro Grand Splendid, 14 May 1919

stops.name: Grand Splendid, the studio in the house
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unrecorded
stops.campa: Glücksmann installs a recording studio inside the theatre, and from 1920 Gardel cuts his Odeon records in the same building he sings in from the stage. Under one roof on Avenida Santa Fe: the film that is projected, the voice that is performed, and the wax the voice is cut into. Nobody has yet decided that these are three separate industries requiring three separate companies. For as long as the decision goes unmade, all three belong to one man who began by carrying another man's glass plates.
suggested_refs: The Odeon recording studio inside the Grand Splendid, from 1920

stops.name: Radio Splendid, the signal
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Radio Splendid begins transmitting from inside the theatre. A fourth thing is now made at this address: sound that goes out over the air to people who paid nothing at a door and own no gramophone. Glücksmann holds film, stage, disc and broadcast in one building on Avenida Santa Fe, in a decade when neither law nor habit says a man may not hold all four. The city hears itself in its own accent for the first time, transmitted from a room above a cinema he built for something else.
suggested_refs: Radio Splendid, first broadcast 23 May 1923, Av. Santa Fe 1860

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the first Concurso del Disco Nacional
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month, day and venue unrecorded
stops.campa: He launches the Concurso del Disco Nacional, a competition for composers and performers that is also, exactly, an engine for selling his own pressings. The hall is not named in the sources consulted. The instinct is the one that made him pay royalties twenty years before anyone else: pay the musicians, make the musicians famous, hold the record of the famous. Seven editions will run in the capital. The tango takes prizes at a contest owned by the house that presses the tango.
suggested_refs: Concurso Nacional del Disco, Buenos Aires editions 1924-1930

stops.name: Montevideo, the contest crosses the river
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month, day and venue unrecorded
stops.campa: The contest is carried over to Montevideo, the first of two Uruguayan editions, three years after it began in Buenos Aires. The venue goes unnamed in the record. What crosses is the format, and with it an assumption that hardens into a fact: that the tango belongs to both banks of the Plata, and that a Uruguayan singer and an Argentine singer compete in the same contest, are pressed by the same house and sold from the same catalogue. Nobody argues, because the catalogue is the argument.
suggested_refs: Montevideo editions of the Concurso del Disco Nacional, 1927 and 1928

stops.name: Montevideo, the second edition
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month, day and venue unrecorded
stops.campa: A second Montevideo edition closes the Uruguayan run, and the contest goes home to Buenos Aires for the rest of its life. Nine editions in two cities, one label standing behind all of them. The prizes are forgotten and the category is not. The music comes to be remembered as neither strictly Argentine nor strictly Uruguayan but Rioplatense, and that category is shaped by which performers one Buenos Aires firm chose to record and which contests it chose to hold.
suggested_refs: Rioplatense tango repertoire in the Disco Nacional catalogues of the 1920s

stops.name: Montaneses 2130, the plant in Belgrano
stops.date_confidence: month and year attested; day unrecorded
stops.campa: In Belgrano, on a plot at Montaneses 2130 to 2150, a factory is completed for the Argentine Talking Machine Works: sixteen hundred and ninety square metres under roof, drawn by the architect Paul Ploetz. Here are pressed the discs his labels sell across four countries. The building does not exist any more, and no source consulted says when it came down or why. The plant survives as an address, an architect's name and a figure in square metres. The quarter around it is now the Barrio Chino.
suggested_refs: Paul Ploetz, factory for The Arg. Talking Mach. Works, Montaneses 2130/50, November 1928

stops.name: Grand Splendid, the first sound films
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unrecorded
stops.campa: The first sound films shown in Argentina are shown in his theatre. Glücksmann has spent thirty-two years importing silent machines, and now the machines talk, and the talking arrives first in the room he built for an orchestra and a screen together. Within a few years the stage and the pit of the Splendid are redundant. The man who ordered the country's first Gaumont camera out of a Paris catalogue is also the man who puts its successor on a screen here before anyone else does.
suggested_refs: First sound film exhibition in Argentina, Grand Splendid, 1929

stops.name: Radio Splendid, Gardel on the air
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the first of October Carlos Gardel makes his radio debut, broadcasting from Radio Splendid inside the theatre. Twelve years after signing him to a recording contract, Glücksmann's building carries that voice out to listeners who own no gramophone at all, only a receiver. Four weeks later the New York market collapses. The thing assembled over thirty-two years, halls in four countries, a plant in Belgrano, a theatre and a station on one avenue, starts to come apart at an edge.
suggested_refs: Carlos Gardel's radio debut, Radio Splendid, 1 October 1929

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the halls sold
stops.date_confidence: the sale is attested as a consequence of the 1929 crash; no source gives a month, and November is placed as following the October collapse
stops.campa: The crash reaches Buenos Aires and Glücksmann sells the cinemas: the whole circuit, sixty halls or a hundred depending which account is read, across Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay and Chile, built up over twenty-one years and let go in far less. He keeps the records, the plant, the theatre and the station. It is the single retreat in forty years of expansion, and the sources treat it as arithmetic rather than as a change of ambition. He is fifty-four, and he does not begin again.
suggested_refs: Divestiture of the Glucksmann exhibition circuit after 1929

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the seventh contest
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month, day and venue unrecorded
stops.campa: The seventh and last Buenos Aires edition of the Concurso del Disco Nacional is held, six years after the first. The cinema circuit is being sold off around it; the contest sits on the side of the business he has chosen to keep. The venue is not named in the sources consulted, as none of the seven venues are. The contests leave behind a decade of Argentine and Uruguayan songwriting entered, judged, pressed and catalogued by one house, which is to say kept.
suggested_refs: Final Buenos Aires edition of the Concurso del Disco Nacional, 1930

segments.name: Nacional-Odeon, and the Taking of the Archive

stops.name: Templo Libertad, the disputed gift
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the sole basis is a grandson's recollection printed in Clarin in 2000, giving a span of 1925 to 1942; the year here is the opening of that span, and the congregation's own history does not corroborate it
stops.campa: On Calle Libertad, facing Plaza Lavalle, stands the synagogue whose cornerstone was laid in September 1897 and which is rebuilt entire in 1932. One tradition, resting on a grandson's recollection printed in a newspaper long after both men were dead, has Glücksmann funding construction there between 1925 and 1942. The congregation's own history names Baron Hirsch as the funder of the ground in 1889 and does not mention him at all. The two accounts do not reconcile, and which building on Libertad is meant is not settled either.
suggested_refs: Templo Libertad (CIRA), Libertad 785, cornerstone 27 September 1897, rebuilt 1932
sources: Wikipedia (ES), 'Max Glucksmann' (grandson's testimony, cited to Clarin, 2000)

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the label absorbed
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unrecorded
stops.campa: EMI is formed in London by merger and the Argentine end restructures accordingly: Discos Nacional becomes Disco Nacional-Odeon, and a catalogue built one exclusive contract at a time is folded into a multinational's ledger. Glücksmann is fifty-six, out of the cinema business, still pressing at Montaneses. The merger happens in London. His part in it happens by contract, in the city he has not left in forty-one years. He signs, as he has signed everything, without travelling.
suggested_refs: Formation of EMI (1931) and the reorganisation of Disco Nacional-Odeon

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the archive expropriated
stops.date_confidence: the expropriation is dated only to the period after the 1943 coup in the source; month and day unrecorded
stops.campa: After the coup of 1943 the state expropriates his film archive: twenty thousand metres of positive and nine thousand of negative, the accumulated record of a national cinema shot and collected since 1897, taken for two thousand six hundred pesos. Glücksmann sues. The Supreme Court eventually rules the material was worth a hundred and fifty-five thousand. By then it has been dispersed or lost. He is sixty-nine years old and litigating over the ashes of the trade he founded, and winning, and getting nothing back.
stops.quote: fueron expropiados los archivos del exhibidor y productor Max Glücksmann. La Comisión Nacional de Museos y Monumentos Históricos había apoyado la compra por el Estado de este inmenso reservorio. Después del golpe de 1943 fue expropiado por una miseria, 2600 pesos. Se trataba de 20.000 metros de película positiva y 9000 de negativo. Tras largo juicio iniciado por Glücksmann, la Corte Suprema decidió que su costo llegaba a los 155.000 pesos, pero era tarde: el material fílmico se había dispersado o perdido y es posible que algo del mismo subsista en el Archivo General de la Nación, que también sufrió un incendio hacia 1950.
stops.quote_source: Claudio Espana, Cronica de la destruccion del cine argentino (1998), quoted in Eugenia Izquierdo, 'El Archivo Grafico de la Nacion, primera experiencia institucional de preservacion de patrimonio cinematografico en Argentina', X Jornadas de Sociologia UBA, 2013 (aacademica.org/000-038/594)
suggested_refs: Supreme Court file on the Glucksmann expropriation suit; Archivo General de la Nacion film holdings
sources: Claudio Espana (1998), quoted in Eugenia Izquierdo, X Jornadas de Sociologia UBA, 2013

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the heart attack
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the twentieth of October Max Glücksmann dies in Buenos Aires of a heart attack, seventy-one years old, still directing the record business on the day it happens. Fifty-six of those years were spent in this city, which he reached at fifteen with no Spanish. He leaves a label, a plant in Belgrano, a theatre on Avenida Santa Fe whose film trade he sold seventeen years before, and an archive the state took two years ago. The address at which he dies, house or hospital, is not given in the sources consulted.
suggested_refs: Buenos Aires press obituaries of October 1946

stops.campa: He is buried at the Cementerio Israelita de Ciudadela, out past the western edge of the capital in the partido of Tres de Febrero. The claim rests on a single source and could not be checked against the cemetery's own registers; the exact plot is unrecorded. No account consulted describes the stone, whether it is marked, whether anyone comes. The man who owned as many as a hundred halls in four countries has no monument, and the record does not say what his grave looks like.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, what the nitrate did
stops.date_confidence: attested date of the newspaper article in which the judgment is printed
stops.campa: Thirty-two years after his death a journalist asks in a newspaper where the old Argentine films have gone, and answers his own question: no duplicates were struck, the stock was nitrate, and part of it burned before 1950. What the state took from Glücksmann for two thousand six hundred pesos it did not keep. Some of it may survive in the Archivo General de la Nacion, which had a fire of its own. The first three decades of a country's cinema exist now mostly as a list of titles.

stops.name: Avenida Santa Fe 1860, the last projection
stops.date_confidence: the building ran as theatre and cinema until 1982 and as cinema alone until 1999; the exact closing date is not given in the sources consulted
stops.campa: The house on Avenida Santa Fe runs as theatre and cinema until 1982 and as a cinema alone until 1999, and then it shuts. Eighty years of use, and the two things that made it famous, the dome and the boxes, have been irrelevant to its business for most of them. It stands empty on one of the busiest avenues in the city, with Orlandi's allegories over a dark floor: a building too expensive to run and too admired to pull down. Nobody in Buenos Aires calls it Glücksmann's any more.

stops.name: El Ateneo Grand Splendid, the bookshop
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The Ilhsa group leases the building in February and spends three million dollars turning it into a bookshop under the architect Fernando Manzone, keeping the dome, the balconies and the stage curtain. It opens in December with a hundred and twenty thousand titles over four thousand square metres. The Guardian calls it the second most beautiful bookshop in the world in 2008; National Geographic calls it the first in 2019. Almost nobody who photographs the ceiling knows whose theatre it was.

stops.name: Casa Lepage, the plaque on Bolivar
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the plaque is attested but the source gives no installation date, and the year here is a placeholder within the period the source describes
stops.campa: On Bolivar the city government has fixed a plaque to the building where the fifteen-year-old took work handling another man's plates. No source consulted gives the year it went up. There is no statue of Max Glücksmann in Buenos Aires, no street carrying his name, no purpose-built memorial: what marks him is a plaque on a shop front and a ceiling in a bookshop, both of them buildings he walked into on business. Of the four countries his halls once covered, nothing else carries the name.
